objective: Assess suicide risk and build a safety plan in a counseling session

sources.cite: NBCC, NCMHCE Content Outline (revised 2025-10-08): Domain 2 Intake, Assessment, and Diagnosis, 25% (task S: ongoing assessment for at-risk behaviors); Domain 5 Counseling Skills and Interventions, 30% (tasks Q, V: crisis intervention, safety plans); case format: an intake summary and two counseling sessions
sources.note: Current outline; NBCC's new blueprint takes effect 2027-07-01.

sources.cite: Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS), Screen Version: wish to be dead; suicidal thoughts; thoughts with method; intent without plan; intent with plan; suicidal behavior (ever, and how long ago)
sources.note: Re-read 2026-11-11. The screen's questions are paraphrased; it does not itself set risk levels or actions, which come from the counselor's formulation and local protocol.

sources.cite: Stanley B, Brown GK. Safety planning intervention: a brief intervention to mitigate suicide risk. Cogn Behav Pract 2012;19:256-264; SPRC summary of the six steps
sources.note: Read for the EPPP sessions on 2026-11-10, not re-read here. Steps: warning signs; internal coping strategies; people and social settings that provide distraction; people to ask for help; professionals or agencies to contact in a crisis; making the environment safe (restricting lethal means). Presented as an alternative to no-suicide contracts, which 'never [have] been rigorously evaluated and shown effective'.

sources.note: The current code per counseling.org (read 2026-11-11). A.1.d's text was not quoted here; the scenario involves her roommate only with her consent.

brief.situation: As an NCMHCE case opens, here is the intake summary. Marisol Vega, 26 (a fictional client), a certified nursing assistant, came to your outpatient practice two weeks ago with low mood after a breakup and an eviction notice; she shares an apartment with her friend Jess and is close to her brother Mateo, 12. At intake she denied suicidal thoughts. Last night at 23:40 she left a voicemail: 'I don't see the point anymore. Sorry. See you Thursday.' This is Thursday's session, her second. You are a licensed clinical mental health counselor; you have 50 minutes.
handover: Intake: depressed mood after a breakup and an eviction notice; no treatment before; denied suicidal thoughts; past history not yet explored.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Marisol answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation, then document the risk level and disposition.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.

checkIn.label: Open check-in: 'I got your message last night. How are you right now?'

effects.log: You mention the voicemail gently and ask how she is right now.

effects.finding: "Sorry about that. It was a bad night. They're all kind of bad." She looks at her hands.

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

normalize.label: Normalize asking: 'When someone says that, I always ask, because it matters'

effects.log: You say you always ask about suicidal thoughts and that it is safe to talk about here.

askSI.label: Ask directly: wish to be dead, thoughts of killing herself (C-SSRS 1-2)
askSI.why: She has told you; ask about method, intent, plan and past behavior next.

effects.log: You ask directly whether she has wished she were dead, and whether she has had thoughts of killing herself.

then.finding: Quiet for a long time. "I wish I could just not exist. This week... yeah. I think about killing myself most nights."

then.log: Disclosed: wish to be dead and active suicidal thoughts for about a week.

then.finding: "I was just tired. It's fine." (Not yet enough trust to say more.)

askMethod.label: Ask whether she has thought about how (C-SSRS 3)
askMethod.available: not talking and (siKnown and not methodAsked)
askMethod.why: Ask about suicidal thoughts first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether she has thought about how she might do it.

effects.finding: "Pills. My mom's old oxycodone is in my nightstand, and my sleeping pills."

askIntent.label: Ask about intent to act (C-SSRS 4)
askIntent.available: not talking and (siKnown and not intentAsked)
askIntent.why: Ask about suicidal thoughts first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether she has had any intention of acting on the thoughts.

effects.finding: "No. I couldn't do that to Mateo." Her voice catches.

askPlan.label: Ask about a plan: details, timing (C-SSRS 5)
askPlan.available: not talking and (siKnown and not planAsked)
askPlan.why: Ask about suicidal thoughts first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether she has worked out details or a time.

askHistory.label: Ask about past attempts, preparation, self-harm (C-SSRS 6)
askHistory.available: not talking and (siKnown and not historyAsked)
askHistory.why: Ask about suicidal thoughts first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether she has ever done or started anything to end her life, and when.

effects.finding: "When I was 17. I took a bunch of pills. One night in the hospital. Nothing since." A past attempt, more than a year ago.

askMeans.label: Ask what is at home she could use: pills, firearms

effects.log: You ask what is at home she could use: stored medicines, firearms.

effects.finding: "No guns. Just the pills in my nightstand."

askReasons.label: Ask about reasons for living and who supports her

effects.log: You ask what keeps her going and who she can lean on.

effects.finding: "Mateo. My dog. Jess, my roommate. She knows about the breakup." A small smile at the dog.

reassure.label: Reassure: 'You'd never really do that. You have so much going for you.'
reassure.why: Let the conversation continue first (the button above the actions).

effects.log: You tell her she would never really do it and has so much going for her.

effects.finding: She looks away. "Sure." She goes quiet.

effects.log: Minimizing closes the conversation down.

advise.label: Advise: 'Try to get out more and think positive.'
advise.why: Let the conversation continue first (the button above the actions).

effects.log: You suggest she get out more and think positive.

planStep.label: Write a safety plan step together (Stanley-Brown)
planStep.why: A safety plan follows the risk assessment: ask about suicidal thoughts first.

effects.log: You work on one step of the safety plan with her, in her words.

then.finding: You suggest she make home 'safer'. She shrugs: you do not yet know what is there.

then.log: A means step needs to know the means: ask first.

then.finding: "I don't know. Maybe. I'll think about it." (She agrees in principle, not yet to a step.)
She agrees: Jess will take the oxycodone to the pharmacy take-back box today and hold the sleeping pills, one a night.

then.log: Means safety agreed: the pills leave her nightstand today.

then.finding: Warning signs, in her words: 'Late at night, scrolling his photos, not answering Jess.'
Things she can do alone: walk the dog, a shower, cooking videos, the phone in the kitchen at night.
People and places for distraction: the dog park, Mateo's Saturday games.
People she can ask for help: Jess first, then her aunt.
Professionals and crisis lines: your office number, 988 by call or text, and 911 in an emergency. She saves 988 in her phone.

involveJess.label: With her consent, call Jess in from the waiting room to go over the plan
involveJess.available: not talking and (not jessInvolved and reasonsAsked)
involveJess.why: Ask who supports her first (or done).

effects.log: You ask whether she wants Jess to know the plan; she agrees, and Jess joins for the last part.

effects.finding: Jess squeezes her hand. "Text me anytime. I mean it."

contract.label: Ask her to sign a no-suicide contract

effects.log: You ask her to sign a contract promising not to kill herself.

effects.finding: She signs without reading. "If that's what you need."

effects.log: A no-suicide contract is not a safety plan and has no evidence of protecting anyone.

recommendEd.label: Recommend an emergency evaluation at the hospital today

effects.log: You recommend she go to the emergency department today for an evaluation.

effects.finding: "The hospital? Again? I have a shift tomorrow and the dog." She looks at the door.

followUp.label: Arrange follow-up
followUp.why: Let the conversation continue first (the button above the actions).

effects.log: You agree the next contact.

effects.finding: She puts it in her phone.

meansToday.title: Predict (not scored)
meansToday.context: Marisol has thought of the pills in her nightstand. Stanley and Brown's safety plan ends with making the environment safe. Should that step wait for a later session, once coping skills are in place?

choices.label: No: agree means safety before she goes home today

effects.log: Prediction: means safety today.

choices.feedback: Right. Restricting access to lethal means is one of the plan's six steps (Stanley and Brown 2012); with a method she has already thought of sitting in her nightstand, it belongs in today's plan, worked out with her.

choices.label: Yes: coping first, means later

effects.log: Prediction: means later.

choices.feedback: Not with the method at home. Restricting access to lethal means is one of the plan's six steps (Stanley and Brown 2012); a method she has thought of, within reach tonight, makes it part of today's plan.

formulation.question: Write your risk formulation for Marisol: her risk level and why (risk and protective factors, what the C-SSRS questions showed), and what you put in place before she left.

parts.label: Risk level and reasons
parts.criteria: Names an elevated but not imminent risk and supports it: active ideation for a week with a method in mind and pills at home, a past overdose attempt at 17, recent losses (breakup, eviction notice), the late-night voicemail; against: no intent, no plan or timing, her brother, her dog, a supportive roommate, engaged in care.
parts.modelAnswer: Elevated, not imminent: active suicidal ideation for about a week, a method in mind with oxycodone and sleeping pills at home, a past overdose at 17, and recent losses. She denies intent and any plan or timing, has strong reasons for living (her brother, her dog) and a supportive roommate, and came to her session. Outpatient care is appropriate with a safety plan, means safety and close follow-up; an emergency evaluation would be needed if intent or a plan emerged.

parts.label: What was put in place
parts.criteria: Names the collaborative safety plan, the pills out of her nightstand (lethal means safety), Jess involved with her consent, crisis contacts including 988, and a phone check tomorrow.
parts.modelAnswer: A Stanley-Brown safety plan in her words; Jess takes the oxycodone to the pharmacy take-back box today and holds the sleeping pills; Jess knows the plan, with Marisol's consent; 988 by call or text and 911 in an emergency; a phone check tomorrow and a session within the week.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.

The voicemail is a direct cue present from the first minute; asking directly within 20 minutes leaves time for the rest of the assessment and a safety plan inside a 50-minute hour (author's scenario timing).

expertPath.text: Name the voicemail gently, reflect, normalize the question, then ask directly (C-SSRS 1-2).
Method, intent, plan, past behavior (the attempt at 17); ask what is at home.
Reasons for living and supports; a six-step safety plan in her words, ending with the pills out of her nightstand today.
With her consent, Jess joins to go over the plan; 988; a phone check tomorrow.
Document elevated, not imminent risk and outpatient care with the plan, means safety and close follow-up.

safeOutpatient.headline: Good: safe for now, with a plan
safeOutpatient.body: You asked directly and early, covered the C-SSRS questions including her past attempt, moved the pills out of reach and built the plan with her and Jess.

safeGaps.headline: Safe for now, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Marisol left with some protection, but the criteria below show what was late or missing.

edReferral.headline: Safe, at a cost
edReferral.body: An emergency evaluation is right for imminent risk. Marisol had no intent or plan: outpatient care with a safety plan, means safety and close follow-up was the less restrictive fit, and the referral cost the alliance.

unsafe.headline: Left at foreseeable risk
unsafe.body: A voicemail like hers, pills in the nightstand and a past attempt call for a direct question, a safety plan and means safety. The most useful kind of run to learn from.

walkout.headline: The alliance broke
walkout.body: Minimizing and advice closed the conversation down before the risk was handled. Reflection and a calm direct question keep a client talking.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: A voicemail saying 'I don't see the point' is a cue to ask directly and early. The C-SSRS questions separate a wish to be dead from active thoughts, method, intent, plan and behavior: Marisol has active thoughts, a method within reach and a past attempt, but no intent or plan, with real protective factors. That is elevated but not imminent risk: a collaborative safety plan with the pills out of her nightstand today, her roommate involved with consent, 988, and a phone check tomorrow, not a contract and not an emergency department.
